summary.text: Electric charge is a property of matter that makes it feel a force in an electromagnetic field, and it comes in two kinds, positive and negative.
Like charges push apart and unlike charges pull together, while an object with no net charge is called neutral.
In ordinary matter electrons carry negative charge and protons carry positive charge, so an excess of either decides an object's overall charge.

items.prompt: You rub a balloon on your hair and the balloon ends up with a negative charge. What is true of your hair?

options.label: It is left with an equal amount of positive charge
It stays neutral, since only the balloon was changed
It gains the same negative charge as the balloon has
It loses its protons, which move over to the balloon

items.explain: Rubbing moves charge from one material to the other, leaving an opposite charge of the same size behind.

items.prompt: A neutral atom picks up one extra electron. What is it now?

options.label: A positive ion, because it has gained something
A negative ion, because electrons outnumber protons
Still a neutral atom, just a slightly heavier one
A new element, because its electron count changed

items.explain: With more electrons than protons the atom carries a net negative charge, which makes it a negative ion.

items.prompt: Two balloons each carry a negative charge and are hung close together. What do they do?

options.label: They drift together, since charged things attract
They ignore each other, as both are the same sort
They push away from each other
They swing together then spring apart repeatedly

items.explain: Charges of the same sign repel one another.

items.prompt: A scientist measures the charge on a tiny free-floating speck. Which total could it be, in units of the elementary charge?

options.label: One and a half units
A third of a unit
Two and a half units
Three whole units

items.explain: Free charges come only in whole multiples of the elementary charge.

items.prompt: Inside a sealed, insulated box you rub a glass rod with silk. Compared with before, what happens to the box's total charge?

options.label: It grows, since rubbing makes new charge
It shrinks, since some charge leaks into the air
It stays the same, as charge only shifts around
It doubles, since both objects become charged

items.explain: In an isolated system the total charge does not change; rubbing only moves charge between the objects.

items.prompt: Quarks carry fractions of the elementary charge. Why do we never see a lone object with a third of that charge?

options.label: Quarks only exist combined, in particles with whole-number charges
Fractional charge is too weak for any instrument to detect
Quarks cancel each other out and leave no charge at all
Quarks turn into electrons whenever they are separated

items.explain: Quarks are found only inside particles whose total charge is a whole multiple of e, and free quarks have never been seen.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong; which?

steps.text: Rubbing glass with silk leaves the glass rod positively charged.
Before rubbing, both were neutral, so the total charge was zero.
In a closed system the total charge must stay at zero afterwards.
So the silk must still be neutral, since only the rod changed.

beats.explain: With a positive rod and a total of zero, the silk has to carry an equal negative charge.

beats.idea: Rubbing never creates charge; it moves it, leaving equal and opposite amounts on the two objects.

paragraphs.heading: Two kinds of charge
paragraphs.text: Electric charge is a property of matter that makes it feel a force when it sits in an electromagnetic field. It comes in two kinds, positive and negative. Charges of the same kind push each other away, and opposite charges pull together. An object with no overall charge is called electrically neutral.

paragraphs.heading: Who carries it
paragraphs.text: In ordinary matter, electrons carry negative charge and protons, in the nuclei of atoms, carry positive charge. A piece of matter with more electrons than protons is negative, one with fewer is positive, and one with equal numbers is neutral. The charge of a large object is just the sum of the charges of its particles. That total is often small, because atoms usually hold equal numbers of protons and electrons, so their charges cancel.

paragraphs.heading: Charge comes in steps
paragraphs.text: Charge is quantized: it comes only in whole-number multiples of a tiny unit, the elementary charge e. One e is about 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C. The proton carries +e and the electron carries −e. Quarks have smaller charges, in steps of 1/3 e, but they are only found joined into particles whose total charge is a whole multiple of e. Michael Faraday was the first to notice that charge comes in separate pieces, in his electrolysis experiments. Robert Millikan's oil drop experiment later showed it directly and measured e.

paragraphs.heading: It never disappears
paragraphs.text: In an isolated system, the total charge stays fixed. Subtract all the negative charge from all the positive charge, and the answer never changes over time. The Standard Model treats charge as a quantum number that is conserved absolutely.

paragraphs.heading: Ions
paragraphs.text: When an atom, or a cluster of atoms, loses electrons, it ends up positive and is called a cation. One that has gained electrons ends up negative, and is called an anion. Both are ions. Ions made from a single atom are monatomic, while those made from two or more bonded atoms are polyatomic.

paragraphs.heading: Static electricity
paragraphs.text: When an object carries a net charge that is not moving, we call it static electricity. Rubbing two different materials together, like amber with fur or glass with silk, makes it easily. Charge moves from one material to the other and leaves behind an equal and opposite charge. Before electrons and protons were discovered, Benjamin Franklin defined positive charge as the charge a glass rod picks up when rubbed with silk.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring charge
paragraphs.text: The SI unit of charge is the coulomb, C, named after the French physicist Charles-Augustin de Coulomb. Electrical engineers often use the ampere-hour instead. Physicists and chemists also count charge in elementary charges. Chemists use the Faraday constant too, equal to the charge carried by a mole of elementary charges.
